subject: using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density

messages.author: 5ea4fdd6f7e361d3
messages.subject: using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density
parts:
Hi all,
When studying rare species, it can be difficult to collect enough sightings to fit a detection function reliably.  I recently did a systematic, small-boat line transect survey for marine mammals.  Observers stayed on effort and collected sightings on both planned (designed) transects and along transit legs.  I’m trying to conduct an analysis in Distance 6.2 (Release 1) in which I use all sightings for fitting the detection function, but only the effort and sightings from the planned transects for estimating encounter rate and density.  I am not sure whether this gets done in Distance using data filters (i.e., I have coded the data so that all of the “transit-leg” sightings were assigned to a transect called Transect 0, so maybe I should be filtering Transect>0 for estimating density), or stratification (i.e., I have set up a “planned” stratum and a “transit-leg” stratum — and maybe I should simply ignore the abundance in the transit-leg stratum).  

This is slightly embarrassing, because I’ve written about this in previous collaborative studies, but in both cases, the analyses were done by co-authors who are statisticians doing the analyses in R.  In one, we had extra sightings, but we also had so few sightings that we had poor power to choose among models.  In that case, we used the extra sightings, but also model averaged on the detection function (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006320709000500 ).  In another case, the primary purpose was to collect ID photos and biopsy samples, so having much more search effort in the high-density area than the low-density area required us to use density surface models (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2011.01656.x/abstract).  

The current study used a systematic survey design, but it was an inefficient one.  We have so many transit-leg sightings that we have to use them to have any hope of estimating esw.  It’s important for this study that we do the analysis in Distance, because we want to share the data and Distance project with other Distance users.  I’ve searched in the Google Group help pages for “transit-leg” sightings, “extra” sightings, “additional” sightings…  I can’t find anything, so I know I’m overlooking something obvious.  I have a vague recollection of this coming up in the context of the pooling robustness properties of distance sampling in the context of stratified surveys, but that workshop was many years ago and I don’t know how to tell Distance to use all sightings for fitting the detection function, but only a subset for estimating abundance. 

Thanks in advance for your help,
Rob

messages.author: 8fbbf490c07a1909
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density
parts:
Hi Rob 

Using the MRDS module of Distance 6.2 you can create a detection function using all of the observations, then employ it in a new analysis filtered so that only your on-transect data (effort, observations) are used. You just need to point distance to the detection function from the analysis employing all data. 

Cheers 

Stewart

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density
parts:
Hi Rob,

Thanks for the question, and to Stewart for his answer.  Stewart is right, but it's also possible to do it using the CDS or MCDS engine - and this is probably easier for single platform data. 

As you suggested, the trick is to set up a separate stratum for your off-effort sightings.  The key thing is to set the area to zero.  Line length is not allowed to be zero, but so long as you use a positive value it doesn't matter what you set that to.  Then, set up an analysis where you estimate the detection function globally (i.e., pooling both the off effort stratum and any other strata you have) and density by stratum as well as globally.  (To do this, in Model Definition, Estimate tab, tick "User layer type Stratum" and under Quantities to estimate, tick Density Global and Stratum, and Detection function Global.(If you're using the MCDS engine, rather than CDS, you would tick Detection function Global and Stratum) )  Set the Global density estimate to be the mean of the stratum-level estimates, weighted by Area (this is the default in the Estimate tab.)

When you run the model, you'll get a warning that the Area=0 for your off-effort stratum, but you can ignore that.  Distance will use all the detections for fitting the detection function, which is what you want.  It will give you a nonsense encounter rate and density estimate for the off-effort stratum, but you don't care about that -- you only care about your on-effort stratum.  If you have more than one on-effort stratum (i.e., a stratified survey) the global density estimate is correct (i.e., ignores the off-effort stratum) because you set the area to zero. The global density is a weighted average of the stratum-level estimates with the weight being the area, and so the weight for this stratum is zero.

Hope this helps.  I couldn't find this tip in the manual, so it's been helpful that you've asked and so we can document the answer in this group. 

Cheers, Len
